title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
text:
The federal minimum wage is still $7.25 per hour, the same rate set in July 2009. I knew it had not changed for a long time, but I wanted to see how different that number looks once inflation is taken into account.
I use monthly FRED data to look at the minimum wage in three ways. First, I plot the nominal federal minimum wage since 1938. Then I adjust it for inflation. Finally, I ask a simpler counterfactual question: if the $7.25 rate from July 2009 had only kept pace with CPI, where would it be now?

title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
text:
The federal minimum wage is still $7.25 per hour, the same rate set in July 2009. I knew it had not changed for a long time, but I wanted to see how different that number looks once inflation is taken into account.
I use monthly FRED data to look at the minimum wage in three ways. First, I plot the nominal federal minimum wage since 1938. Then I adjust it for inflation. Finally, I ask a simpler counterfactual question: if the $7.25 rate from July 2009 had only kept pace with CPI, where would it be now?

title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
text:
Data
I downloaded two monthly series directly from FRED using the fredr package: the federal minimum wage (FEDMINNFRWG) and the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPIAUCNS).
I originally planned to express the real minimum wage in 2025 dollars. While checking the data, I found that the October 2025 CPI observation was missing in the FRED data I downloaded. Rather than use an incomplete year as the base, I switched to 2024, which has all twelve monthly observations.
The real minimum wage is calculated as:
\[
\text{Real Minimum Wage}_t
=
\text{Nominal Minimum Wage}_t
\times
\frac{\text{Average CPI in 2024}}{\text{CPI}_t}
\]
This puts wages from different years into the same purchasing-power units.

title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
section: How Has the Nominal Minimum Wage Changed?
text:
How Has the Nominal Minimum Wage Changed?
The first figure shows the federal minimum wage in current dollars.





Federal minimum wage in current dollars, 1938–2026.




The step pattern is what I would expect from a policy variable. The wage stays fixed for long periods and then jumps when a new federal rate takes effect.
One detail I noticed from the monthly data is that the minimum wage was still $6.55 in June 2009 and increased to $7.25 in July. It has remained at $7.25 ever since.
That $7.25 line looks flat after 2009, which is exactly why I wanted to adjust it for inflation.

title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
section: What Changes After Adjusting for Inflation?
text:
What Changes After Adjusting for Inflation?
The second figure shows the same minimum wage after converting it to 2024 dollars.





Federal minimum wage adjusted to 2024 dollars.




The highest real value in the series occurs in February 1968, when the $1.60 federal minimum wage was worth about $14.68 in 2024 dollars.
After that, the real series repeatedly rises when the nominal minimum wage is increased and then falls as prices continue to increase. By August 2026, $7.25 had a real value of only about $6.79 in 2024 dollars.
What surprised me more was that the peak came all the way back in 1968. The nominal wage has gone up since then, but that does not mean workers at the federal minimum wage can buy more with it.

title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
section: What If $7.25 Had Kept Up with Inflation?
text:
What If $7.25 Had Kept Up with Inflation?
I then used July 2009 as a starting point and asked what the federal minimum wage would look like if it had increased at the same rate as CPI.
\[
\text{Inflation-Adjusted Wage}_t
=
7.25
\times
\frac{\text{CPI}_t}{\text{CPI}_{July\ 2009}}
\]





Actual federal minimum wage compared with a CPI-adjusted version of the July 2009 wage.




Both lines begin at $7.25 in July 2009. After that, the actual federal minimum wage stays flat while the CPI-adjusted line keeps rising.
By August 2026, maintaining the purchasing power of the July 2009 wage would require about $11.28 per hour. The actual federal minimum wage was still $7.25.
I use $11.30 only as a purchasing-power comparison, not as an estimate of what the minimum wage should be.

title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
text:
Takeaway
I already knew the federal minimum wage had been stuck at $7.25 since 2009. What I didn’t expect was how much its purchasing power had fallen. In 2024 dollars it’s now worth less than half of what it was in 1968.
One caveat is that I only looked at the federal rate, and plenty of states set a higher one, so this isn’t what every minimum-wage worker actually faces. Next time I’d want to bring state minimums in.

title: How Much Has the Federal Minimum Wage Lost in Purchasing Power?
text:
Source
Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, FRED.
The data were downloaded directly in R using the fredr package.
Series used:

Federal Minimum Hourly Wage (FEDMINNFRWG)
Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPIAUCNS)

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
There are a lot of things someone interested in data or AI could spend time learning. Python and SQL are obvious examples, but there are also cloud platforms, databases, machine learning libraries, and newer tools related to LLMs.
Instead of looking at another list of “top skills,” I wanted to see what employers were actually mentioning in job posts.
My question was:
I used R and rvest to scrape the September 2026 Hacker News “Who is hiring?” thread.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Getting the Data
The Hacker News thread works well for this because the job posts are available directly on the webpage and do not require a login.
I first downloaded the page and saved a copy of the HTML.

library(rvest)
library(here)
library(xml2)

hn_url <- "https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49522897"

page <- read_html(hn_url)

raw_html_file <- here(
  "data",
  "raw",
  "hn_who_is_hiring_sep2026.html"
)

xml2::write_html(
  page,
  raw_html_file
)

Saving the HTML was useful because I could keep working with the same version of the page instead of downloading it again every time I ran the code.
I then selected the comment rows from the page.

comment_rows <- page |>
  html_elements("tr.athing.comtr")

Hacker News includes both original job posts and replies underneath them. I used the comment indentation level to remove the replies and keep only the top-level posts.
After doing that, I had 261 hiring posts.
One thing to keep in mind is that one post can advertise more than one position. Because of that, I treat each company post as one observation rather than each individual job opening.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
section: Finding Data, AI, and ML Jobs
text:
Finding Data, AI, and ML Jobs
My first idea was to search the entire job description for words such as “AI,” “data,” and “machine learning.” The problem is that this can include posts that are not actually hiring for those types of roles.
For example, a company could mention AI when describing its product but only be hiring a general software engineer.
To make the filter more specific, I only looked at the first 350 characters of each post. The beginning usually contains the company name and the positions being advertised.
I then searched that section for titles such as Data Scientist, Data Engineer, Data Analyst, Machine Learning Engineer, AI Engineer, and Research Scientist.

jobs_raw <- jobs_raw |>
  mutate(
    role_zone = str_sub(text, 1, 350)
  )

data_jobs <- jobs_raw |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      role_zone,
      data_role_pattern
    )
  )

This left me with 39 Data, AI, or ML-related hiring posts out of the original 261.
The filtering was done automatically using the same rule for every post.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Which Technologies Show Up Most?
For those posts, I searched the full text for a set of technologies such as Python, SQL, AWS, GCP, PostgreSQL, Docker, Kubernetes, PyTorch, and LLMs.
I counted each technology only once per post. So if one company mentioned Python several times, it still only counted as one Python observation.
Here is what I found:





Technologies mentioned most often in Data, AI, and ML-related Hacker News hiring posts.




Python stands out pretty clearly. It appeared in 19 of the 39 posts, or about 48.7%.
LLMs were second at about 35.9%.
GCP, PostgreSQL, and PyTorch each appeared in about 12.8% of the posts.
One result I did not expect was SQL. The exact word “SQL” only appeared in about 7.7% of the posts.
That does not mean SQL is unimportant. Some companies listed PostgreSQL or Snowflake instead of explicitly writing “SQL.” I kept them separate because I wanted the results to reflect what was actually written in the posts.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
What I Would Learn First
If I were using these results to decide what to study, Python would be the easiest place to start. It showed up in almost half of the relevant posts and can be used across data science, machine learning, and data engineering.
The number of LLM mentions also stood out to me. More than one-third of the posts mentioned LLM-related technology, which shows how common it has become in this particular group of tech companies.
After Python, I would probably focus on a mix of database and cloud skills rather than trying to learn every machine learning library at once. PostgreSQL, GCP, AWS, and Azure all appeared in the sample.
For someone more interested in AI and machine learning specifically, PyTorch and experience working with LLMs also seem useful based on these postings.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Limitations
This is a fairly small sample. It only uses one month of Hacker News job posts, and Hacker News has a lot of startups and technology companies. The results should not be treated as a picture of the entire job market.
The posts also come from different countries, so this is not specifically a study of U.S. employers.
Another limitation is that a technology appearing in a post does not always mean it is required. Sometimes companies describe their current tech stack even when they are not asking applicants to already know every tool.
Finally, my filter depends on specific job titles. A relevant job with an unusual title could be missed.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Takeaway
For this Hacker News sample, Python was by far the most commonly mentioned technology in Data, AI, and ML-related hiring posts. LLMs also appeared surprisingly often, while cloud platforms, databases, and machine learning tools showed up across a smaller share of posts.
The main thing I took from this is that looking directly at job postings can be more useful than relying on generic lists of “skills you need.” It gives a more concrete idea of what companies are actually mentioning right now.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Source
Hacker News, Ask HN: Who is hiring? (September 2026).

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
One of the most common misunderstandings in statistics is the meaning of a p-value. Suppose a researcher runs a hypothesis test and obtains a p-value of 0.03. It is tempting to say that there is only a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true. However, this interpretation is incorrect.
A p-value answers a different question.
Suppose the null hypothesis is denoted by (H_0). The p-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one in our data, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. In simplified notation,
[ p = P( H_0). ]
The important part is the condition “(H_0) is true.” The p-value does not directly tell us
[ P(H_0 ), ]
which would be the probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing the data. These two probabilities may look similar, but they answer very different questions.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
A Coin Example
Imagine that we want to determine whether a coin is fair. Our null hypothesis is
[ H_0: p = 0.5, ]
where (p) is the probability of getting heads.
Now suppose we flip the coin 20 times and observe 18 heads. If the coin is actually fair, the probability of getting 18 or more heads is only about 0.02%.
That makes 18 heads look very unusual under the assumption that the coin is fair.
The p-value captures exactly this idea. It asks:

If the coin really were fair, how likely would it be to observe a result this extreme or even more extreme?

If we are doing a two-sided test, we would also count outcomes that are equally extreme in the opposite direction, such as getting 2 or fewer heads.
A very small p-value therefore suggests that the observed data are difficult to reconcile with the null hypothesis.
However, even a very small p-value does not prove that the null hypothesis is false. It only tells us that the data would be unusual if the null hypothesis were true.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
section: What a p-Value Does Not Mean

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
What Does 0.05 Mean?
A common convention is to call a result “statistically significant” when the p-value is below 0.05. This cutoff is useful as a rule of thumb, but it is not a magical boundary between truth and falsehood.
A p-value of 0.049 and a p-value of 0.051 represent almost the same amount of evidence, even though one may be labeled statistically significant and the other may not.
This is why researchers should not focus only on whether a p-value crosses the 0.05 threshold. Effect sizes, confidence intervals, sample size, and the economic meaning of the result also matter.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
Why the Concept Feels Unintuitive
The p-value is easy to misunderstand because people naturally want to ask:

“Given the data, how likely is my hypothesis to be true?”

But the p-value asks the reverse question:

“Assuming my hypothesis is true, how unusual are these data?”

That reversal in conditioning is the main reason the concept is unintuitive.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
The Main Takeaway
The easiest way to remember the meaning of a p-value is:

A p-value measures how surprising the data are under the null hypothesis.

It does not measure the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.
A p-value is therefore one piece of evidence about how well the data fit a hypothesis, not a direct probability that the hypothesis is right or wrong.

title: How Unequal Was the COVID-19 Unemployment Shock Across Education Groups?
text:
COVID-19 caused a sudden disruption in the U.S. labor market, but the effect was not evenly distributed across workers. One difference that stands out is education.
In this post, I use IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) data to look at how unemployment changed across education groups before, during, and after the COVID-19 shock. I also compare age groups to see whether the education gap was concentrated among younger workers or appeared more broadly.
I focus on adults ages 25 to 64 and divide education into four groups: less than high school, high school, some college or an associate’s degree, and a bachelor’s degree or higher.

title: How Unequal Was the COVID-19 Unemployment Shock Across Education Groups?
text:
COVID-19 caused a sudden disruption in the U.S. labor market, but the effect was not evenly distributed across workers. One difference that stands out is education.
In this post, I use IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) data to look at how unemployment changed across education groups before, during, and after the COVID-19 shock. I also compare age groups to see whether the education gap was concentrated among younger workers or appeared more broadly.
I focus on adults ages 25 to 64 and divide education into four groups: less than high school, high school, some college or an associate’s degree, and a bachelor’s degree or higher.

title: How Unequal Was the COVID-19 Unemployment Shock Across Education Groups?
text:
Data
The data come from the monthly IPUMS CPS from 2015 through 2024. I use age, education, employment status, year, month, and the CPS final person weight (WTFINL).
I restrict the sample to ages 25–64 because most people in this age range have already completed their education but are still of working age.
All unemployment rates are weighted using the CPS sampling weights. I calculate the unemployment rate as the weighted number of unemployed workers divided by the weighted labor force:
\[
\text{Unemployment Rate}
=
\frac{\text{Weighted Unemployed}}
{\text{Weighted Employed} + \text{Weighted Unemployed}}
\]
People who are not in the labor force are not included in this calculation.

title: How Unequal Was the COVID-19 Unemployment Shock Across Education Groups?
text:
Unemployment Before and After COVID
The first figure shows annual unemployment rates by education from 2015 to 2024.

Before COVID-19, unemployment was falling for all four education groups. However, there was already a clear gap by education. Workers with less than a high school education consistently had the highest unemployment rate, while workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher had the lowest.
That pattern became much more noticeable in 2020. Unemployment increased sharply for every group, but the increase was much larger among workers with less education.
After 2020, unemployment fell quickly again. By 2022 and 2023, the rates were much closer to their pre-pandemic levels, although the ordering across education groups remained similar.

title: How Unequal Was the COVID-19 Unemployment Shock Across Education Groups?
text:
What Happened in 2020?
Annual averages hide how sudden the change was, so the second figure looks at monthly unemployment rates from 2019 through 2021.

The shock appears very clearly in the spring of 2020.
In April 2020, the unemployment rate was about 20.8% for workers with less than a high school education and 17.0% for high school graduates. The rate was around 14.6% for workers with some college or an associate’s degree.
For workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher, it was much lower at about 7.9%.
This is probably the clearest result in the data. The pandemic increased unemployment across the entire labor market, but workers with lower levels of education experienced a much larger increase. The gap also did not disappear immediately once unemployment started falling.

title: How Unequal Was the COVID-19 Unemployment Shock Across Education Groups?
text:
Does Age Change the Pattern?
The last figure compares the change in unemployment between April 2019 and April 2020 for different age and education groups.

I use April in both years so that the comparison is not driven by normal seasonal differences between months.
There is some variation across age groups, but the education pattern is much more consistent. Workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher experienced a smaller increase in unemployment in every age group.
Workers with only a high school education, some college, or less than a high school education generally experienced much larger increases. The size of the shock changes somewhat with age, but the education gap is not limited to young workers.
This suggests that the relationship between education and the COVID unemployment shock was present across much of the working-age population.

title: How Unequal Was the COVID-19 Unemployment Shock Across Education Groups?
text:
Conclusion
The CPS data show that the COVID-19 unemployment shock was very unequal across education groups.
Workers with less education had higher unemployment even before the pandemic, but the differences became much larger during the spring of 2020. In April 2020, unemployment exceeded 20% among workers without a high school diploma, compared with less than 8% among workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher.
The age comparison shows that this was not just a pattern among younger workers. Across age groups, workers with more education generally experienced a smaller increase in unemployment.
These results are descriptive, so they do not mean that education itself caused the difference. Education is related to many other characteristics, including occupation, industry, and the ability to work remotely. Still, the CPS data make one point clear: the employment effects of the COVID-19 shock were far from evenly distributed.
Source: IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS). Population estimates use CPS sampling weights.
